newsitem.title: UK: Short stg seen good value once confidence returns.
newsitem.headline: Short stg seen good value once confidence returns.

text.p: The knee-jerk sell-off in short sterling following the Bank of England's hawkish inflation report is overdone and the front contract is a bargain at current levels, analysts said on Wednesday.
But until unpredictable market sentiment improves, the short sterling strip remains a no-go area.

"There's value here. If you can hang on and take the pain I'm sure there's a good profit there," said one trader. "But it's very difficult to pick the bottom. As soon as we think it's hit it, it goes down a few more ticks and we get burnt."

The March short sterling contract took fright at the Bank of England's tough November inflation report on Wednesday. By 1400 GMT, it stood at 93.34, 10 basis points lower than Tuesday's close and 14 basis points down from early Wednesday trade.
This implies three-month money rates -- which trade close to base rates -- will be 6.66 percent by the end of the first quarter next year.
Since last week's surprise quarter-point rate rise, taking base rates to 6.00 percent, the March contract has shed 43 basis points.
While the Bank's quarterly report said a further rise in UK interest rates was likely to be necessary, analysts agreed a 50 basis point or more rise by March next year was highly unlikely.
"The Chancellor may hike again by 25 basis points but that's probably about it," said GNI financial analyst Mark Henry.

"December short sterling is certainly a buy. If you look at the timing of the next monetary meeting...there's no way there's going to be a rate hike before the end of the year." The next monthly monetary meeting is December 11.
By 1403 GMT, December short sterling was down six basis points at 93.63 implying three-month rates of 6.37 percent by the end of the year -- equating to a further quarter-point on official rates.
But until market sentiment turns around, analysts said no amount of logic would entice short sterling higher.
"If you stand back and look at the levels implied by the short sterling strip, one has to say they are being unduly pessimistic," said Union Discount chief economist Philip Shaw.
"Ultimately there is probably some value in the front two contracts, but it would be a brave person that comes into the market with the psychology as negative as it is at the moment."
Analysts said there may be some downside to the market yet, as stop loss orders are triggered and investors remain edgy.
"But if it goes much lower then there will be a certain amount of bargain hunting. I don't think it's going to go very much lower," said Shaw.

Analysts said the market was looking for something to snap it out of the doldrums. They said a firm date for the UK general elections, which must be held by May 1997, new data giving clues on inflationary pressures in the economy, or the November 26 budget could provide that trigger.

GNI's Henry said if the Chancellor adopted a lax fiscal stance in the budget, the market may interpret the latest rate rise as a move for that purpose. "Short sterling would take that quite badly," he said.

One trader said the market would only be appeased by a reasonable signal that rates will not go up before an election. "I think the markets are wrong. I don't think the Chancellor is going to put rates up again before the election," he said.
"But we need to see some figures to back that up."
